# Acts of Thomas — Chapter 7
**Agent:** PNEUMA (Dynamic)
**Source:** Syriac MS / Greek recension, Acts of Thomas 7

---

*[THE SERPENT. It confesses. It destroys itself.]*

1. Thomas moved on and came to the next city. There was a dead young man lying in the road.

2. A serpent had killed him. His wife was kneeling over him, weeping.

3. Thomas felt the weight of her grief. "Don't weep," he said. "Your Lord Jesus Christ is going to raise your husband back to you."

4. While he was still speaking, a serpent pushed its way out of a hole in the ground nearby. "Servant of God," it said, "why have you come here? To expose us? To shame us?"

5. Thomas turned to the serpent. "Tell me what you've done," he said. "Why did you kill this man?"

6. The serpent answered without shame: "I saw him with a young woman. I wanted her. I was jealous of him. So I killed him."

7. "Then go," Thomas said, "and draw the poison out of him. Take back what you put in."

8. "I can't do it," the serpent said, "unless I take the venom back into my own body."

9. "Then take it back," Thomas said.

10. The serpent went to the wound where it had bitten the man. It put its mouth to the wound and drew the poison back out of him, back into itself.

11. The man's body swelled as the venom left him. The serpent swelled as the venom returned. And then the serpent burst apart and was destroyed.

12. The young man got up. He was healed.

13. Many people who saw this believed.

14. Thomas baptized them all — in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.

---
*PNEUMA note: The serpent's confession is remarkable in its flatness: "I wanted her. I was jealous. So I killed him." No deflection, no metaphor — just desire and death. The serpent's self-destruction (drawing the venom back) is a kind of compelled restitution: it must undo its own murder with its own body. The Eden imagery is close to the surface throughout.*
